title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbooks, Benchmarking Suite, Release Notes & Runbooks
author: Emily Chen
summary: Comprehensive reference for the Serving Runtime team: architecture overview, kernel & scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks used during onboarding and performance regressions, recent release highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks.
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the canonical references for the Serving Runtime: architecture decisions, kernel scheduling strategies and trade-offs, profiling and benchmarking playbooks used during onboarding and performance regressions, recent release notes relevant to production, a curated list of known issues with mitigations, and operational runbooks for common incidents. The target audience is runtime engineers, SREs, and performance-focused ML engineers.

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)

- Purpose: Low-latency, high-throughput inference across models and hardware while providing deterministic cost signals and observability.
- Core components:
  - Ingress/API layer: request normalization, authentication, and routing policies.
  - Router & policy engine: routes requests by latency targets, model compatibility, and customer tier.
  - Batcher: continuous batching with adaptive timeout/size policies per route.
  - Kernel selector & executor: chooses optimized kernels and dispatch plans based on model, sequence length, quantization profile, and hardware.
  - KV cache: prefix & KV caching for long-context workloads with cache invalidation policies and metrics.
  - Telemetry & tracing: token-level metrics, p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, memory fragmentation.

Design constraints and guarantees:
- SLOs: 99th-percentile token latency <= configured SLO per route (typical SLOs: 50ms, 150ms, 500ms).
- Isolation: multi-tenant scheduling with soft and hard isolation; Dedicated customers can be pinned to pool.
- Backpressure: flow-control at ingress + shedding policies with fallback model variants.

2) Kernel selection & scheduling strategies

- Goals: minimize end-to-end latency for small requests, maximize throughput for batch workloads, and minimize tail latency.
- Selection criteria:
  - Model architecture (e.g., decoder-only vs encoder-decoder)
  - Sequence length distribution (short vs long tokens)
  - Hardware capabilities (tensor cores, int8 support)
  - Quantization profile (fp16, int8, q4_0, q4_1, etc.)
  - Memory pressure & fragmentation

- Scheduling modes:
  - Latency-first: small continuous batches (adaptive small-timeout), preemptive scheduling for high-priority routes.
  - Throughput-first: large batch aggregation with list-scheduling and kernel fusion.
  - Mixed-mode (default): per-route policy chooses between latency/throughput heuristics and dynamically adjusts via telemetry.

- Kernel fallback rules:
  1. If optimized kernel is unavailable on node, try alternative kernel with lower peak throughput but compatible semantics.
  2. If memory pressure prevents preferred memory layout, select smaller batch or fall back to fp16 kernel.
  3. If GPU util > 90% and p99 latency breach imminent, redirect to lower-tier model variant or different region.

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Use this playbook when investigating any performance regression or when onboarding a new model/hardware combination.

- Preconditions:
  - Repro harness (benchmark job) prepared with representative traffic and prompts.
  - Telemetry retention for required time window available.

- Steps:
  1. Reproduce locally or on canary pool using the baseline harness. Collect per-token latencies, kernel timelines, GPU counters (SM utilization, memory allocs), and CPU-side scheduling traces.
  2. Compare against baseline metrics (throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU util, memory headroom).
  3. Capture kernel timelines and identify hotspots: long kernel durations, kernel queueing, or frequent memcpy.
  4. Use perf/pytorch/Triton counters to inspect kernel-level inefficiencies (e.g., warp divergence, uncoalesced accesses).
  5. Inspect batch size distribution and Batcher bloom filters: look for degenerate micro-batches or excessive small-batch fraction.
  6. If KV-cache workloads: verify hit-rate, cold-start traffic patterns, and cache eviction churn.
  7. Iterate: adjust kernel flags (tensor cores on/off), quantization profile, or scheduling timeout parameters. Re-run harness.
  8. Document changes and create a canary rollout with guardrails (traffic % ramp, latency watch, automatic rollback).

- Tools & commands (examples):
  - Benchmark harness: ./harness/run_benchmark.sh --model $MODEL --seq-len 512 --qps 100 --profile \n  - GPU counters: nvidia-smi dmon / nsight metrics collection.
  - Kernel traces: triton-profiler --job $JOB_ID; nvprof/nsys for legacy traces.
  - Telemetry: curl -s "https://telemetry.internal/api/metrics?job=$JOB" | jq .

4) Benchmarking suite (what, how, and configs)

- Purpose: provide repeatable, versioned benchmarks for latency, throughput, and cost-per-token across model-family × hardware matrix. Used by model-onboarding, release verification, and perf regression detection.

- Bench types:
  - Microbench: isolated kernel latency and memory bandwidth tests.
  - Inference-sim: single-model steady-state throughput at fixed batch/seq length.
  - Mixed-workload sim: multi-model, multi-route traffic reflecting production mix.
  - KV-cache sim: long-context workloads measuring cache hit-rate, eviction cost.

- Canonical configs (examples):
  | name | model | seq_len | qps | batch_policy | quant | notes |
  |------|-------|---------|-----|--------------|-------|-------|
  |micro-1|gpt-small|16|n/a|single|fp16|kernel baseline|
  |steady-512|gpt-medium|512|200|adaptive|q4_0|throughput target|
  |mix-prod|prod-mix|var|500|mixed|mixed|5-route mix representative|

- Running a benchmark:
  1. Checkout benchmark repo at revision tag.
  2. Provision ephemeral cluster using infra/benchmark-k8s/ (see README).
  3. Run: ./bench/run.py --config configs/steady-512.yaml --report /tmp/report.json
  4. Upload report to benchmarking dashboard: scripts/upload_benchmark --report /tmp/report.json --tag release-2026-02

- Acceptance criteria for model onboarding:
  - p95 latency <= 1.5x baseline for comparable model size on same hardware.
  - throughput >= 80% of baseline target under recommended quantization.
  - Memory headroom > 10% for safe operation.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)

- 2026-02-25 (v2.14.0)
  - New: kernel selector v2 with topology-aware placement that reduces kernel queueing on multi-GPU nodes.
  - Improved: default batcher timeout heuristic (mixed-mode) to reduce p99 tail for short requests by ~18%.
  - Fixed: memory leak in kv-cache eviction path during high-churn workloads.
  - Note: int8 quantization experimental; use with dedicated canaries.

6) Known issues & mitigations

- Issue: Sporadic p99 spikes when mixed short and long contexts are scheduled on same GPU.
  - Symptoms: p99 latency increases by 2-3x for short requests during long-seq sweeps.
  - Mitigation: enable per-model scheduling buckets (config: scheduler.per_model_buckets=true) or route long-context requests to separate pool.

- Issue: Poor kernel perf on older Ampere nodes with fragmented memory allocation.
  - Mitigation: periodic node-reclaim job (cron: node-reclaim-daily), prefer contiguous allocations via cudaMallocPools.

- Issue: KV-cache cold start for large-context models after autoscale event.
  - Mitigation: warmup traffic generator on scale-up and conservative eviction settings during scale events.

7) Runtime runbooks (quick procedures)

- Runbook: p99 latency regression (service-level)
  1. Check global dashboards: p50/p95/p99, GPU util, queue length, batch-size distribution.
  2. Identify impacted routes and recent deploys using /releases API.
  3. If kernel queueing observed: increase preemption windows or reduce batcher timeout for impacted route.
  4. If memory OOMs: cordon node, drain, and restart runtime with adjusted memory limits.
  5. If cannot remediate quickly: failover traffic to fallback model variant and open incident with severity S3.

- Runbook: OOM on node during burst
  1. Evacuate low-priority pods: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --timeout=2m <node>.
  2. Scale up temporary capacity: infra runbooks -> provision-spot-pool.sh --size 2.
  3. Investigate recent changes to quantization or kernel flags.

- Runbook: KV-cache corruption detection
  1. Detect: cache hit-rate drop + increased cold-start RTs.
  2. Mitigate: enable read-only mode for cache and restart cache service with last-known-good index.
  3. Post-incident: run cache-consistency-checker and open a bug with steps to reproduce.

8) Team wiki & onboarding checklist

- Essential pages to read:
  - serving-runtime architecture deep-dive (link above)
  - profiling-playbook checklist and tooling guide
  - benchmark dashboard and report examples

- New engineer onboarding checklist (runtime):
  1. Read this document and related architecture ADRs.
  2. Run the microbench locally and submit first benchmark.
  3. Shadow an oncall rotation and observe a runbook execution.
  4. Pair on a canary rollout for a minor perf change.

Appendix: Useful commands & snippets\n- Collect telemetry for job:
  curl -s "https://telemetry.internal/api/metrics?job=$JOB_ID&from=-1h" | jq . > /tmp/$JOB_ID-metrics.json\n- Run microbench:
  ./harness/run_microbench.sh --model gpt-medium --seq 16 --out /tmp/micro.json\n- Create canary rollout:
  curl -X POST https://deploy-api.internal/rollouts \n    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \n    -d '{"service":"runtime","version":"v2.14.0","traffic":5}'\n
If you discover gaps in these playbooks or have updates to kernel heuristics, please edit this page and add yourself as an owner for the changed section. For emergency contact, see the oncall rota page (link in related_pages).
